title: Bidriware
description: Bidriware is the signature metalcraft of Bidar: a zinc-and-copper alloy inlaid with hammered silver and blackened with a paste of soil from the Bidar fort, made the same way for almost five centuries.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Bidar · Since c. 1500

items.value: Zinc-and-copper alloy, inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire
A paste of soil from the Bidar fort
The inlay technique is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list

blocks.html:
Bidriware is the signature metalcraft of Bidar, made the same way for almost five centuries. A vessel of zinc-and-copper alloy is cast, scored with a steel point, inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire, and then dipped in a paste of soil from the Bidar fort that turns the alloy a deep matte black — leaving the silver inlay untouched and gleaming against it. No other metalwork looks like it.

I · The Craft Bidar · Five Centuries

Black metal inlaid with silver

Casting, scoring, inlay, and the blackening paste unique to Bidar

The craft takes its name from Bidar, the only place it has ever been made. A vessel is cast in an alloy of zinc and copper, its surface scored with a steel point in a pattern, then inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire set into the scored lines. The vessel is finally dipped in a paste made from soil taken from within the Bidar fort itself, which reacts with the alloy to turn it a deep matte black — while leaving the silver, untouched by the reaction, standing out bright against it.

II · Recognition A Craft Made Nowhere Else

Continuing tradition

Still practised by Bidar's karigars, and internationally recognised

Bidriware remains in production in Bidar today, carried on by the same families of karigars who have practised it for generations. The inlay technique is included on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, recognition of a craft that, despite its fame across the Deccan and beyond, has never been successfully replicated anywhere else — the blackening reaction depends on the particular soil of the Bidar fort itself.

references.text: George Michell & Mark Zebrowski, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates (The New Cambridge History of India I.7), Cambridge University Press, 1999.
